The '''Khalsa Diwan Society Vancouver''' ('''KDS'''; {{Langx|pa|ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਦਿਵਾਨ ਸੋਸਾਇਟੀ ਵੈਨਕੂਵਰ}}) is a [[Sikh]] [[gurdwara]] organization in [[Vancouver]], [[British Columbia]], [[Canada]].

Founded in 1906, it is the oldest Sikh society in [[Greater Vancouver]],<ref name="PGCp31">Pang, Guek-cheng. ''Culture Shock! Vancouver''. [[Marshall Cavendish International Asia Pte Ltd]], August 15, 2010. {{ISBN|9814484806}}, 9789814484800. p. [https://books.google.com/books?id=cTOJAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA31 31].</ref> and its original location was the largest gurdwara in [[North America]]. The current gurdwara is located at the intersection of Southwest [[Marine Drive (Greater Vancouver)|Marine Drive]] and Ross Street,<ref name="NayarSikhSpacep46">Nayar, "The Making of Sikh Space," p. [https://books.google.com/books?id=dgtgGhMUgIUC&pg=PA46 46].</ref> in [[South Vancouver]].<ref name="NayarSikhSpacep48">Nayar, "The Making of Sikh Space," p. [https://books.google.com/books?id=dgtgGhMUgIUC&pg=PA48 48].</ref>

== History ==
The Khalsa Diwan Society was founded on July 22, 1906, and was registered on March 13, 1909.<ref>{{Cite web |title=History: Khalsa Diwan Society |url=http://kdsross.com/about/history/khalsa-diwan-society/ |access-date=16 October 2024 |website=Khalsa Diwan Society}}</ref>
[[File:Group photo of Sikh men at the Second Avenue Gurdwara, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, ca.1910.jpg|thumb|Group photo of Sikh men at the Second Avenue Gurdwara during its opening day, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, 19 January 1908]]
Their first site and [[gurdwara]] was built in 1908 at 1866 West 2nd Avenue, inaugurated on January 19. The financial situation of the Society depended on the number of [[Sikhs]] living in [[British Columbia]], and donations rose considerably as more Sikhs came to the province. The population of Sikhs rose in the period of 1904–1908 to 5,185, but fell to 2,342 in 1911. The Sikh population dwindled even more, to 1,099, as the year 1918 approached.{{citation needed|date=November 2014}} Verne A. Dusenbery, Professor of Anthropology and Chair of the Global Studies Program at [[Hamline University]] in [[Minnesota]], wrote that the gurdwara served as "truly a religious, social, political, cultural, and social service center for the entire South-Asian immigrant population of the [[Lower Mainland|lower mainland]]" during its early history.<ref name=":0">Dusenbery, Verne A. 1981."Canadian Ideology and Public Policy: The Impact on Vancouver Sikh Ethnic and Religious Adaptation." ''Canadian Ethnic Studies'' 13(3):104-105. Winter.</ref>

In the 1940s, the KDS served in a leadership role as Indo-Canadians demanded for voting rights, and it did so in a secular capacity.<ref>Johnston, Hugh, p. 5-6.</ref> The gurdwara had a homeless shelter and a ''langar'' or kitchen.<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=105}} The KDS had a secular social role as a community centre and also served [[Hinduism in Canada|Hindus]] and [[Islam in Canada|Muslims]] among the Indo-Canadian community. Raj Hans Kumar stated that in political affairs the KDS represented all "Hindus", which at the time meant all people of [[Indian people|East-Indian]] origin.<ref>Hans, Raj Kumar. 2003. "Gurdwara as a Cultural Site of Punjabi Community in British Columbia, 1905 – 1965." Pp. 227-228 in ''Fractured Identity: The Indian Diaspora in Canada'', edited by Sushma J. Varma and Radhika Seshan. Jaipur: Rawat Publications.</ref>

In the early 1950s, a serious split occurred in the Canadian Sikh community, when the Khalsa Diwan Society elected a [[Kesh (Sikhism)|clean-shaven Sikh]] to serve on its management committee.<ref name="PRMagocsi_Canada">{{cite book
 | editor = Paul Robert Magocsi
 | title = Encyclopedia of Canada's Peoples
 | origyear = 1998
 | year = 1999
 | publisher = University of Toronto Press
 | isbn = 978-0-8020-2938-6
 | oclc = 56300149
 | pages = 1157
}}</ref> Although most of the early Sikh immigrants to Canada were non-[[Khalsa]], and a majority of the members of the society were clean-shaven non-Khalsa Sikhs, a faction objected to the election of a non-Khalsa to the management committee. The factions in Vancouver and [[Victoria, British Columbia|Victoria]] broke away from the Khalsa Diwan Society, and established their own gurdwara society called the Akali Singh Society, which opened in 1952.<ref name="PRMagocsi_Canada" /><ref name="JohnstonHughp6">Johnston, Hugh. 1988. "The Development of Punjabi Community in Vancouver since 1961." ''Canadian Ethnic Studies'' 20(2).</ref>{{Rp|page=6}}

By the late 1950s, there were plans to establish [[Punjabi language|Punjabi-language]] schools for Canadian-born children and to collect funds for a new community centre.<ref>Srivastava, Ram P. ([[University of Calgary]]). "Family Organization and Change among the East Indians of British Columbia, Canada." In: Kurian, A. (editor). ''Family in India: A Regional View''. 1972 (The Hague). p. 369-391. CITED: p. 377-378.</ref> In 1963, the Society began planning for a new gurdwara and community centre.<ref name="JohnstonHughp6" />{{Rp|page=6}}

The Society purchased {{convert|2.75|acre|m2}} of city land in 1968 at the intersection of Southwest [[Marine Drive (Greater Vancouver)|Marine Drive]] and Ross Street,<ref name="NayarSikhSpacep46" /> in [[South Vancouver]].<ref name="NayarSikhSpacep48" />

Construction began in winter 1969,<ref name="JohnstonHughp7">Johnston, Hugh, p. 7.</ref> and was completed in the first week of April 1970 for a price of $6,060. Sri [[Guru Granth Sahib]] was moved from the 2nd Avenue gurdwara to the Ross Street gurdwara on the day of [[Vasakhi]] 1970.{{citation needed|date=November 2014}} The initial plans asked for a library and community centre, but these aspects were eliminated from the plans. The celebration for [[Guru Nanak]]'s 500th birthday was held prior to the grand opening in 1970.<ref name="JohnstonHughp18">Johnston, Hugh, p. 18.</ref> The building was intended to look like a [[Nelumbo nucifera|lotus]] rising from water. To get inspiration for the style, the architect, [[Arthur Erickson]], traveled to [[Agra]] and [[Amritsar]].<ref name="JohnstonHughp7" />

In 1979, the annual income of the KDS was $300,000.<ref name="JohnstonHughp19">Johnston, Hugh, p. 19.</ref> The membership, which came with a $12 membership fee, had been around 5,000 prior to 1979. After the elimination of the fee, membership increased.<ref name="JohnstonHughp18" /> That year the leadership of the gurdwara changed.<ref name="JohnstonHughp89">Johnston, Hugh, p. 8-9.</ref> Previously, the KDS was controlled by [[Indian Marxism|Marxist Sikhs]] who did not practice Sikhism.<ref name="NayarMissp2223">Nayar, "Misunderstood in the Diaspora," p. 22-23. "For instance, the [[World Sikh Organization]] (WSO) gained control over the Khalsa Diwan Society in South Vancouver, which had previously been run by non-practising ‘comrade’ Sikhs (that is, those who have a Marxist orientation)."</ref>  According to Kamala Elizabeth Nayar, in 1984, the pro-[[Khalistan]] [[World Sikh Organization]] (WSO) began controlling the gurdwara.<ref name="NayarMissp2223" /> According to Hugh Johnston, Vancouver Sikhs stated that the political bloc that took charge of the KDS Gurdwara network by 1979 consisted of about 10-15 families.<ref name="JohnstonHughp89" />

=== Khalsa Diwan Road ===
[[File:Khalsa Diwan Road.jpg|alt=Street sign of Khalsa Diwan Road|thumb|192x192px|Street sign of Khalsa Diwan Road with the KDS Vancouver Gurdwara in the background|left]]
As part of an initiative by [[Vancouver City Council]] to commemorate prominent members of the community, Ross Street was alternatively named Khalsa Diwan Road in 2018. Additional street signs marking it as Khalsa Diwan Road were added at from the Gurdwara at SW Marine Drive to 57th Avenue in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/vancouver-public-spaces-new-names|title=15 public spaces have been named after prominent Vancouver residents|last=Chan|first=Kenneth|date=2018-09-21|website=Daily Hive|language=en|access-date=2019-07-20}}</ref>

==Branches==
In the 1960s, the main gurdwara was in Vancouver and the branch gurdwaras were in [[New Westminster]], [[Abbotsford, British Columbia|Abbotsford]], [[Victoria, British Columbia|Victoria]], and Port Alberni.<ref name="JohnstonHughp6" />{{Rp|page=5}}

By 1973, the cities with KDS temples were Abbotsford, [[Mesachie Lake, British Columbia|Mesachie Lake]], New Westminster, [[Paldi, British Columbia|Paldi]], [[Port Alberni]], and Vancouver.<ref name="AmesConflictp20">Ames, and Inglis, "[http://ojs.library.ubc.ca/index.php/bcstudies/article/download/789/832 Conflict and Change in British Columbia Sikh Family Life]," p. 20.</ref> However the New Westminster Khalsa Diwan became its own Sikh society the following year.<ref name="JohnstonHughp6" />{{Rp|page=18}}

In 1975 the Khalsa Diwan Society of Abbotsford also separated, as the title of the Abbotsford gurdwara was transferred to the separated entity. The Abbotsford Sikhs wanted to have local control over their gurdwara, the [[Gur Sikh Temple]].<ref>"[https://carleton.ca/india/wp-content/uploads/Budh-Singh-Kashmir-Kaur-Dhahan.pdf Budh Singh and Kashmir Kaur Dhahan]" ([https://web.archive.org/web/20150413164352/http://carleton.ca/india/wp-content/uploads/Budh-Singh-Kashmir-Kaur-Dhahan.pdf Archive]). [[Carleton University]]. Retrieved on April 13, 2015.</ref>

==Events==
Every March, a celebration of the martyrdom of [[Mewa Singh Lopoke]] is held. Sikhs from California go to the KDS to celebrate the event.<ref>Haar, Kristen and Sewa Singh Kalsi. ''Sikhism'' (Religions of the World Series). [[Infobase Publishing]], January 1, 2009. {{ISBN|1438106475}}, 9781438106472. p. [https://books.google.com/books?id=YOI1nB_zTyAC&pg=PA86 86].</ref>
